questions.prompt: A churn team runs a grid search over 4 learning rates, 3 tree depths and 2 subsample values, scoring every combination with 5-fold cross-validation. After the search, they refit the best combination once on all the data. How many models are trained in total, counting that final refit? Give a whole number.
questions.explanation:
First count the combinations: 4 × 3 × 2 = 24. Each combination is trained once per fold, so cross-validation alone needs 24 × 5 = 120 fits. The final refit on all the data adds 1, giving 121.

The usual mistakes are stopping at 24, which forgets that each combination is trained once per fold, or stopping at 120, which forgets the refit. Another slip is adding the grid sizes (4 + 3 + 2 = 9) instead of multiplying them. A grid tries every combination, so the sizes multiply. That is why grids grow so fast: adding a fourth setting with 5 values would take the search to 600 fits before the refit.
questions.deeper: This arithmetic is why teams move to random search or Bayesian optimisation once the grid grows. A strong candidate also notes that scikit-learn's GridSearchCV does the final refit by default, and that wall-clock time depends on how many fits run in parallel, not just the total count.

questions.prompt: A tutoring app uses an LLM API to explain maths problems to students in English and in Thai. The team notices that a Thai explanation uses about three times as many tokens as the same explanation written in English. What explains this, and what does it mean for the product?
options: The subword vocabulary was learned mostly from English text, so Thai splits into shorter pieces. Thai sessions cost more and use up the context window sooner.
Thai characters take three bytes each in UTF-8 and every byte is one token, so counts grow. Cost and context limits stay the same because both are counted in words.
The tokenizer splits every language into single characters, and Thai words are longer. Cost stays the same because the API charges a flat price per request.
Token counts differ by language, but the model merges them back into words in its first layer, so cost and context use depend on words, not tokens.
questions.explanation:
Subword tokenizers such as BPE build their vocabulary from the text they were trained on. Languages that were common in that text get long, efficient tokens, while rarer languages get broken into many short pieces, sometimes single characters or bytes. Usage is billed per token and the context window is a token limit, so the same lesson in Thai costs more, takes longer to generate and leaves room for less history.

The UTF-8 option starts from a true fact, since a Thai character does take three bytes. But tokens are learned subword units, not one token per byte, and both price and context limits are counted in tokens, not words. The single-character option is wrong because subword tokenizers keep common words whole, and token-priced APIs do not charge a flat rate per request. The option about merging tokens in the first layer is wrong because every token is its own position in the sequence, so it uses compute and context no matter what the model does with it later.
questions.deeper: In practice, measure token counts on real traffic in each language before setting budgets, limits and prices. A strong candidate also notes that product codes, IDs and some code formats split badly, and that comparing context windows across models needs care, because different tokenizers turn the same text into different token counts.

questions.prompt: A team automates expense-report checks. Every report goes through the same three steps: extract the line items with an LLM, compare them with the travel policy, then file the result in the finance system. A teammate proposes rebuilding it as an agent that decides for itself which tools to call and in what order. Which response is best?
options: Keep the fixed workflow, since the steps never change and a fixed path is cheaper, faster and easier to test.
Switch to an agent, since it can adapt its steps to odd reports, which matters more here than cost or predictability.
Keep the fixed workflow, since an agent cannot write to a system like the finance system without a human.
Switch to an agent, since a fixed workflow cannot use an LLM for a step like extraction and must rely on hand-written rules.
questions.explanation:
In a workflow, your code fixes the path and the LLM is called at set points inside it. In an agent, the model looks at what has happened so far and decides the next action in a loop. That freedom is worth paying for when the path cannot be known in advance, such as debugging an unfamiliar failure or researching an open question. Here every report follows the same three steps, so an agent adds cost, latency, run-to-run variation and new ways to fail, such as skipping the policy check, while gaining nothing.

Adapting to odd reports sounds useful, but here there is nothing to adapt: every report takes the same three steps. The extra freedom brings more room for mistakes and makes testing harder, and odd reports are better caught by a check in the workflow that flags them for review. Agents call external systems all the time, since that is what tools are for, so that option has the right choice for a wrong reason. Workflows can and often do include LLM steps, and this one already uses an LLM to extract line items.
questions.deeper: A strong candidate says "start with the simplest thing that works" and adds agency only where it earns its keep. A common design keeps the main workflow fixed and hands only the reports that fail a check to an agent that can investigate, such as by looking up past receipts.

questions.prompt: To serve a search-query intent classifier on cheaper hardware, you train a small model to match the softened output probabilities of a large, accurate model, along with the true labels. This technique is called ______.
questions.explanation:
In knowledge distillation, a large teacher model's outputs become extra training targets for a small student. The teacher's probabilities are softened with a temperature above 1, so the student sees more than the top answer. For a query labelled laptops, the teacher might say 0.70 laptops, 0.25 laptop accessories and 0.05 phones, which tells the student that laptops and accessories are close. These soft targets carry far more information per example than a hard label, so a small student often gets much closer to the teacher than it would by training on labels alone.

The common mistake is to answer pruning or quantization. Those compress the same model by removing weights or lowering their precision. Distillation trains a separate, smaller model. Another near miss is fine-tuning, which adapts a model to new data but does not involve learning from a second model's outputs.
questions.deeper: In LLM work, distillation often means generating outputs from a large model and fine-tuning a small one on them. A strong candidate notes the limits: the student rarely beats the teacher, it inherits the teacher's errors, and the terms of use of some models restrict using their outputs to train others.

questions.prompt: A clinic uses a model to screen retina photos for a disease that appears in about 2% of patients. A missed case can lead to lasting vision loss. A false alarm costs one short review by a specialist. Which metric should the team put first when comparing models?
options: Recall on the disease class, since each missed patient costs far more than one extra specialist review.
Overall accuracy, since it counts every photo and so reflects both kinds of mistake in one number.
Precision on the disease class, since it keeps specialists from spending their time on healthy patients.
Specificity, since almost all photos are healthy and it measures how well those patients are cleared.
questions.explanation:
The costs here are lopsided. Missing a sick patient can mean lasting harm, while a false alarm only costs a few minutes of a specialist's time. Recall, TP / (TP + FN), measures the share of sick patients the model catches, so it is the metric that tracks the expensive mistake.

Accuracy is dominated by the 98% of healthy photos. A model that calls everyone healthy scores 98% while catching nobody. Precision protects specialist time, which matters, but it is the cheap side of the trade in this setting. You would watch it as a constraint, not optimise it first. Specificity measures how many healthy patients are correctly cleared. It is the negative-class twin of recall and says nothing about how many sick patients were missed.
questions.deeper: A strong answer adds a guardrail: maximise recall subject to a workload limit, such as no more than 50 referrals a day. Interviewers like hearing that you would report recall at a fixed precision or referral rate, because recall alone is easy to max out by flagging everyone.

questions.prompt: You start training an image classifier for product photos. Within the first few hundred steps, the training loss swings up and down wildly, climbs above its starting value, and then turns into NaN. What is the most likely cause?
options: The learning rate is too high, so each update overshoots the minimum and the weights diverge.
The learning rate is too low, so the optimizer stalls and the loss never manages to settle down.
The batch size is too large, so the averaged gradient loses its signal and points the wrong way.
The model is too small, so it lacks the capacity to fit the data and the loss keeps on rising.
questions.explanation:
A learning rate that is too high makes each step jump past the low point of the loss and land somewhere worse. The next step overshoots even further, so the loss oscillates, climbs above where it started, and eventually overflows to NaN. Rising above the starting loss is the telling sign, because a sensible optimizer should not make things worse early on.

A learning rate that is too low gives the opposite picture: a smooth, very slow decline, not wild swings. A larger batch averages more examples, so its gradient is a smoother and more accurate estimate, not a misleading one. It cannot make the loss climb on its own. A model that is too small underfits, which looks like a loss that flattens at a high value, not one that explodes. The usual fix is to cut the learning rate by a factor of 3 to 10, add a warmup period, and consider gradient clipping.
questions.deeper: In interviews, describe the learning-rate range test: train briefly while raising the learning rate step by step, plot loss against learning rate, and pick a value a bit below where the loss starts to blow up. Also mention checking the input pipeline, since a single corrupt batch can cause a similar spike.

questions.prompt: A video app has 50 million videos. Its recommender first pulls a few hundred candidates per user with cheap methods, then scores only those with a large ranking model. What is the main reason for this two-stage split?
options: Running the ranking model on every video for each request is far too slow, so retrieval cuts the pool first.
Ranking models cannot use user features, so a retrieval stage is needed to add personalisation before ranking.
The split removes the need for labels, because retrieval is unsupervised and ranking reuses the retrieval scores.
Two stages give more diverse results, because each stage is trained on a different random half of the history.
questions.explanation:
It comes down to compute per request. Running a large ranking model over 50 million videos every time a user opens the app would take far too long and cost too much. Candidate generation uses cheap methods, such as nearest-neighbour search over embeddings, popular items or co-watch lists, to cut the pool to a few hundred. The expensive model then spends its budget only where it matters.

Ranking models use user features all the time. That is how they personalise, so the claim that they cannot is false. Neither stage removes the need for labels. Both are usually trained on logged clicks or watch time, and the ranker learns from its own labels rather than reusing retrieval scores. Diversity is a real goal, but it is usually handled by a re-ranking step or business rules, not by training stages on random halves of the data.
questions.deeper: A strong candidate adds that the stages are tuned for different goals. Retrieval is judged by recall: did the good items make it into the few hundred? Ranking is judged by precision at the top of the list. Many systems add a light third stage for re-ranking, business rules and diversity.

questions.prompt: A k-nearest neighbours model for a food delivery app uses two features: distance to the restaurant in km (0 to 30) and order value in dollars (5 to 500). Before computing distances between orders, both features should go through ______ so that neither one dominates just because of its units.
questions.explanation:
kNN finds neighbours by Euclidean distance, which adds up squared differences in each feature. A gap of 200 dollars in order value adds 40,000 to the squared distance, while the largest possible gap in km adds only 900. Without scaling, the model is effectively choosing neighbours by order value alone. Scaling puts both features on a similar range, for example by standardising each to mean 0 and standard deviation 1, or min-max scaling to 0 to 1.

The common mistake is to assume the model will learn to weight the features. kNN has no weights to learn. It uses the raw distances, so the units decide importance. Another slip is fitting the scaler on all the data. Fit it on the training rows only, then apply the same transform to validation and live data.
questions.deeper: The same issue hits k-means and SVMs with RBF kernels, which use distances, and PCA, which follows raw variance. Tree models do not care, because splits depend only on the order of values. A strong candidate also notes that outliers can wreck min-max scaling, so a robust scaler using the median and IQR may be safer.

questions.prompt: A rental company screens tenant applications with a model. In group A, 240 of 400 applicants are approved. In group B, 105 of 250 applicants are approved. What is the disparate impact ratio, the lower group's approval rate divided by the higher group's approval rate? Give it as a decimal to 2 places.
questions.explanation:
Compare rates, not counts. Group A's approval rate is 240 / 400 = 0.60. Group B's is 105 / 250 = 0.42. The ratio is 0.42 / 0.60 = 0.70.

The common mistake is to divide the raw counts, 105 / 240 ≈ 0.44. That mixes in the fact that the groups have different numbers of applicants, which says nothing about how each group is treated. Another slip is to put the higher rate on top and get 1.43.

A ratio of 0.70 is below 0.8, the cutoff in the four-fifths rule. That rule comes from US guidance on hiring, not housing, so for tenant screening it is a screening flag many teams borrow, not the legal test. Even in hiring, falling below 0.8 does not prove discrimination. It is a signal to investigate, for example by checking whether the gap comes from features that act as proxies for group membership.
questions.deeper: With small groups, the ratio swings a lot by chance, so strong candidates pair it with a significance test or a confidence interval. Interviewers may also ask what you would do next: look for proxy features, compare error rates by group, and talk to legal before changing anything.

questions.prompt: A subscription app trains a churn model on data where 3% of users churn. Which of these are sound ways to handle the imbalance? Select all that apply.
options: Use class weights so that mistakes on churners cost more in the training loss
Oversample churners in the training set only, after the train and test split
Pick the decision threshold from the precision-recall curve instead of using 0.5
Oversample churners before the split, so the test set is balanced as well
Compare models on accuracy, since balancing the classes makes it a fair metric
questions.explanation:
Class weights make each churner count more in the loss, so the model cannot ignore them to reduce total error. Oversampling the training set after the split has a similar effect by showing the model more churners. A tuned threshold matters because with 3% positives many churners get scores well below 0.5. Choosing the cut from the precision-recall curve lets you pick the trade-off you actually want.

Oversampling before the split is a real mistake. Copies of the same churner can land in both training and test, so the model is graded on rows it has already seen. The test set also stops looking like real traffic, where 3% churn, so every metric you read from it is off. Accuracy stays a poor guide no matter how you train. It is measured on the real test distribution, where predicting "no churn" for everyone still scores 97%.
questions.deeper: Interviewers like hearing that class weights and resampling often act much like a shift in the scores, so a well-chosen threshold on an unweighted model can get much of the same gain. Also mention that oversampling or reweighting distorts predicted probabilities, so recalibrate if the scores are used as real churn chances.

questions.prompt: In a product recommender, two items have embedding vectors a = [1, 2, 2] and b = [2, 0, 1]. What is the cosine similarity between them? Give it as a decimal to 2 places.
questions.explanation:
Cosine similarity is the dot product divided by the product of the two lengths: a·b / (‖a‖ × ‖b‖).

- Dot product: 1×2 + 2×0 + 2×1 = 4
- Length of a: √(1² + 2² + 2²) = √9 = 3
- Length of b: √(2² + 0² + 1²) = √5 ≈ 2.236
- Cosine: 4 / (3 × 2.236) = 4 / 6.708 ≈ 0.596, which rounds to 0.60

The most common mistake is to stop at the dot product and answer 4. The raw dot product grows with the length of the vectors, so it cannot be compared across pairs. Dividing by the lengths removes that effect and leaves only the angle between the vectors, which is why cosine always sits between -1 and 1. Another slip is to compute the Euclidean distance, √((1-2)² + (2-0)² + (2-1)²) = √6 ≈ 2.45. That measures how far apart the points are, not the angle, and a bigger value means less similar.
questions.deeper: Many vector databases store unit-length vectors. Once every vector has length 1, the dot product equals the cosine, so the search can use a plain inner product, which is cheaper. An interviewer may ask what goes wrong if you mix normalized and unnormalized vectors in the same index.

questions.prompt: Six months after launch, an auditor asks your team to rebuild the production fraud model from scratch and show that the rebuilt model matches the one in production. Which set of things must have been versioned at training time to make this possible?
options: Training data snapshot, code commit, config, package environment and random seeds
Code commit, config, package environment, random seeds and the final metrics report
Training data snapshot, code commit, config, random seeds and the model weights file
Training data snapshot, package environment, random seeds and the serving request logs
questions.explanation:
A trained model is the output of a recipe. To get the same output again you need every ingredient: the exact data, the exact code, the settings it ran with, the library versions, and the random seeds that controlled shuffling, initialisation and sampling. Miss any one and the rebuilt model can differ.

The set with the metrics report has no data snapshot. Tables change as rows are added or corrected, so rerunning the same query six months later gives different training data. The set with the weights file skips the package environment. Keeping the weights lets you serve the old model, but not rebuild it, and a library upgrade can change defaults or numerical results. The set with the serving logs has no code commit or config, so you cannot know which features, model type or hyperparameters were used. Serving logs record what the model saw after launch, not what it learned from.
questions.deeper: Even with all five versioned, GPU training can differ slightly between runs because some kernels are not deterministic. A strong answer says what matching should mean: identical weights if you force deterministic settings, or the same metrics within a small tolerance. Tools such as DVC or MLflow are simply ways to record these five things.

questions.prompt: A support bot resolves each incoming ticket on its own with probability 0.7, and tickets are independent of each other. The number of tickets it resolves out of the next 20 follows a ______ distribution.
questions.explanation:
A binomial distribution counts successes in a fixed number n of independent trials, each with the same success probability p. Here n = 20 tickets and p = 0.7, so the count is Binomial(20, 0.7). Its mean is n × p = 14 tickets and its variance is n × p × (1 − p) = 4.2.

The usual mix-up is with Bernoulli. A Bernoulli variable describes one trial, a single ticket resolved or not, and the binomial is the sum of n of them. Another slip is Poisson, which counts events in a fixed interval with no upper limit, such as tickets arriving per hour. Here the count cannot exceed 20, which points to the binomial. Poisson is a good approximation to the binomial only when n is large and p is small, which is not the case here.
questions.deeper: Interviewers often build on this, asking for the chance the bot resolves at least 18 of 20, or how to put a confidence interval on a resolution rate. In production, the independence assumption is the weak point. Tickets from one outage tend to succeed or fail together.

questions.prompt:
Using NumPy 2.x, the rows below are two days and the columns are three ads, holding click counts. What does the last line return? Give a whole number.

```python
import numpy as np
clicks = np.array([[3, 0, 5],
                   [1, 4, 2]])
clicks.sum(axis=0).max()
```
questions.explanation:
`axis=0` collapses the rows, so the sum runs down each column. That gives one total per ad: 3 + 1 = 4, 0 + 4 = 4 and 5 + 2 = 7, so the array is [4, 4, 7]. Its max is 7, the clicks for the best ad across both days.

The common mistake is to read `axis=0` as "add up each row". That is `axis=1`, which gives the daily totals [8, 7] and a max of 8. A rule that helps: the axis you name is the one that disappears. A (2, 3) array summed over axis 0 becomes shape (3,), one value per column.
questions.deeper: pandas follows the same rule: `df.sum(axis=0)` gives one value per column, which is why it is the default. When unsure, print the shape after each step. A common follow-up asks for each row's mean with `keepdims=True`, so the result can be subtracted from the original array by broadcasting.

questions.prompt:
A vision model inspects 1,000 parts on a factory line. Its confusion matrix is:

- Predicted defect, actually defect: 45
- Predicted defect, actually fine: 15
- Predicted fine, actually defect: 30
- Predicted fine, actually fine: 910

What is the model's precision for the defect class? Give it as a decimal to 2 places.
questions.explanation:
Precision asks: of the parts the model flagged as defects, how many really were? The model flagged 45 + 15 = 60 parts. Of those, 45 were real defects. So precision is 45 / 60 = 0.75.

The common mistake is to read the wrong row or column. Dividing by all real defects, 45 + 30 = 75, gives 45 / 75 = 0.60, which is recall. Another slip is to quote accuracy, (45 + 910) / 1,000 = 0.955, which looks strong only because most parts are fine. A simple habit helps: precision uses the predicted-positive counts as its denominator, recall uses the actual-positive counts.
questions.deeper: On a factory line, precision tells you how much good stock the model sends to scrap or re-inspection, and recall tells you how many bad parts reach customers. Interviewers often follow up by asking which of the two the plant manager cares about more, and what that implies for the threshold.

questions.prompt: An A/B test of a new checkout button reports a difference in conversion rate between the two groups with p = 0.03. Which statement correctly interprets this p-value?
options: Assuming no real effect, a difference at least this extreme would appear about 3% of the time.
There is a 3% probability that the new button truly has no effect on the conversion rate.
There is a 97% probability that the new button truly raises conversion compared with the old one.
If the test were run again, about 97% of repeats would also give a significant result.
questions.explanation:
A p-value is computed by assuming the null hypothesis is true, here that the button makes no difference. It is the probability of seeing data at least as extreme as what you saw under that assumption. A small p-value says the result would be surprising if there were no effect, which is evidence against the null.

The option giving a 3% chance that the button has no effect flips the conditional. The p-value is P(data this extreme | no effect), not P(no effect | data), and getting the second needs a prior, as in Bayes theorem. The option claiming a 97% chance the button raises conversion makes the same flip and also ignores direction. The option about 97% of repeats being significant confuses the p-value with statistical power. The chance a repeat is significant depends on the true effect size and the sample size, which this one p-value does not tell you.
questions.deeper: Interviewers like follow-ups on what p = 0.03 does not show: the size of the effect, or whether it matters for the business. A strong candidate reports the effect with a confidence interval, and warns that peeking at results daily or testing many metrics at once makes small p-values far more common by chance.

questions.prompt: In self-attention, each head computes one score for every pair of tokens in the sequence. A summarization service raises its maximum input from 2,000 tokens to 8,000 tokens. By what factor does the number of attention scores per head per layer grow? Give a whole number.
questions.explanation:
With n tokens, every token attends to every token, so each head builds an n × n score matrix with n² entries. At 2,000 tokens that is 4,000,000 scores. At 8,000 tokens it is 64,000,000 scores. The ratio is 64,000,000 / 4,000,000 = 16, which is the same as (8,000 / 2,000)² = 4² = 16.

The common mistake is to answer 4, scaling linearly with length. The parts of a transformer that work on one token at a time, such as the feed-forward layers, do grow linearly, which is why the mistake is tempting. The pairwise score matrix does not. This quadratic growth is the main reason long inputs are expensive in compute, and also in memory when the full matrix is stored.
questions.deeper: A strong candidate adds that methods like FlashAttention avoid storing the full score matrix, which fixes the memory problem but not the quadratic compute. Sparse or sliding-window attention trade some quality for lower cost. During generation, each new token's cost grows linearly with context because of the KV cache, which is a common follow-up.

questions.prompt: A recipe app recommends dishes from user ratings using matrix factorisation. New users and newly added recipes both get poor recommendations. Which strategies help with this cold-start problem? Select all that apply.
options: Ask new users to pick a few cuisines or diets at sign-up and seed their recommendations from those
Score new recipes from their ingredients, text and photo embeddings before any ratings exist
Show each new recipe to a small, controlled share of users so that early ratings for it arrive quickly
Look up each new user's factorisation embedding, which the model fits from their profile at sign-up time
Hide new recipes until they have 100 ratings, so the model only ever ranks items that are well measured
Raise the number of latent factors so the model has enough room to represent new users and new recipes
questions.explanation:
Matrix factorisation learns an embedding for each user and each recipe from their ratings. With no ratings there is nothing to learn from, so cold start needs other signals or a way to gather data fast.

Onboarding questions give a new user a starting profile from day one. Content features let the system score a recipe by what it is, using its ingredients, text and photo, instead of by who rated it. A small exploration budget shows new recipes to some users so real feedback arrives quickly, and it is how many production systems handle new items.

The idea of an embedding fitted from the profile at sign-up is false. Matrix factorisation fits the embedding to a user's ratings, not their profile, and at sign-up there are none, so it would be random or a default vector. More latent factors do not help either. They give the model more capacity to fit existing ratings, but a user or recipe with no ratings still has nothing to fit. Hiding recipes until they reach 100 ratings creates a trap. Hidden recipes cannot be rated, so many will never reach 100 and new content stays invisible.
questions.deeper: A strong answer separates user cold start from item cold start, since the fixes differ. It may also mention hybrid models that blend content features with collaborative signals, so a new item starts from a content-based embedding that moves toward a learned one as ratings arrive. Popular dishes by region are a simple, strong fallback.

questions.subtopic: naming the error of too-simple models
questions.prompt: A straight-line model predicts house prices from floor area alone. Prices really curve upward for large homes, so training and validation error are both high and close together. The bias-variance decomposition splits expected error into three named terms. The term for error that comes from a model being too simple to capture the true pattern is called ______.
questions.explanation:
Bias is the error from wrong assumptions built into the model. A straight line cannot bend, so however much data you give it, it will keep missing the curve for large homes. That is why training error stays high: the model is wrong even on data it has seen. Validation error is close to training error because the model is too simple to memorise anything.

The common mix-up is with variance. Variance is the error from a model being too sensitive to the particular training set, which shows up as low training error and much higher validation error. Some people also answer underfitting. Underfitting is the name of the situation, not one of the three terms. The decomposition is bias squared plus variance plus irreducible noise, and bias is the term that causes underfitting. Adding a squared term or a tree-based model would cut bias here, while more data alone would not help much.
questions.deeper: In interviews, tie the term to a fix. High bias calls for more capacity or better features, not more rows. A useful check is whether training error is far from a reasonable target, such as human-level error or the error of a stronger reference model.

questions.subtopic: choosing a model for tabular data
questions.prompt: A lender wants to predict loan default from 20 applicant features, a mix of numeric and categorical, across 50,000 past loans. The regulator requires a clear reason for every declined application. Which first model is most sensible?
options: Logistic regression, since each coefficient shows how a feature moves the odds of default.
A deep neural network, since deep models reliably beat simpler ones on tabular data of this size.
A random forest of 1,000 deep trees, since averaging many trees makes each decision easy to trace.
A support vector machine with an RBF kernel, since its support vectors give a simple rule per feature.
questions.explanation:
Logistic regression is a strong first model here because it is fast, works well on tabular data of this size, and is easy to explain. Each coefficient says how much a one-unit change in a feature moves the log-odds of default, so you can turn a prediction into reason codes such as high debt-to-income or short credit history. It also gives a baseline that any more complex model must beat.

Deep networks do not reliably beat simpler models on tabular data, and they are hard to explain to a regulator. A forest of 1,000 deep trees is accurate but opaque, since a single prediction passes through thousands of splits, so averaging makes tracing harder, not easier. An RBF kernel SVM works in an implicit feature space, and its support vectors are training examples, not readable rules about features.
questions.deeper: A strong candidate mentions that gradient-boosted trees often win on accuracy for tabular data, and that teams sometimes use them with SHAP explanations. Whether a regulator accepts that is a business and legal question, so starting with an interpretable baseline and measuring the accuracy gap is the safer path.

questions.prompt: A 20-layer fully connected network for churn prediction uses sigmoid activations in every hidden layer. During training, the weights in the first few layers barely change while the last layers learn normally. After the hidden activations are switched to ReLU, the early layers start learning. What best explains both observations?
options: Sigmoid's slope is at most 0.25 and near zero when saturated, so backprop multiplies many small factors. ReLU's slope is 1 for positive inputs, so the gradient keeps its size.
Sigmoid outputs are capped at 1, so large activations get squashed and the loss stops falling. ReLU is unbounded above, so the network can keep lowering the loss with larger activations.
Sigmoid gradients grow as they flow back through many layers, so gradient clipping shrinks the early updates to almost nothing. ReLU keeps each layer's slope at most 1, so clipping never kicks in.
Sigmoid outputs are always positive, so each unit's incoming weight gradients share one sign and the updates zigzag. ReLU removes this sign problem, so the updates point straight downhill.
questions.explanation:
Backpropagation computes the gradient for an early layer by multiplying one factor per later layer, and each factor includes the activation's derivative. The sigmoid's derivative σ(x)(1 − σ(x)) peaks at 0.25 when x = 0 and falls toward 0 when the unit saturates at large positive or negative x. Even in the best case, and ignoring the weight terms, 19 such factors give at most 0.25¹⁹, which is about 4 × 10⁻¹², so the first layers get almost no signal. ReLU's derivative is exactly 1 for any positive input, so active units pass the gradient back without shrinking it.

The option about capping at 1 confuses a bounded output with a vanishing gradient. Boundedness alone does not stop learning, and it would not single out the early layers. The option about growing gradients and clipping has the direction backwards. Sigmoid shrinks gradients, and clipping by norm scales every layer by the same factor, so it could not starve only the early ones. The option about positive outputs names a real but minor sigmoid issue. ReLU outputs are never negative either, so switching to ReLU does not remove it, and it would slow every layer, not just the first few.
questions.deeper: A strong answer also names the other fixes used in practice: initialization suited to the activation, such as He initialization for ReLU, residual connections that give gradients a direct path, and normalization layers. A common follow-up is the dying ReLU problem, where units stuck on negative inputs output zero and stop learning, which variants like Leaky ReLU or GELU ease.

questions.prompt: Scanned invoices go through an LLM that pulls out the supplier name, invoice date and total, and the result is loaded into an accounting system. About 3% of replies fail to parse. Some wrap the JSON in a sentence, and some leave out the total field. What is the most reliable fix?
options: Enforce a JSON schema through structured output or a tool call, then validate each reply and retry the failures.
Add "Return ONLY valid JSON" in capitals to the prompt, then regex out the first brace-delimited block of each reply.
Set the temperature to 0, so the model gives the same well-formed JSON structure every time it reads one of the invoices.
Ask the model for plain text instead, then make a second LLM call that converts that text into JSON before it is loaded.
questions.explanation:
Schema-constrained output limits which tokens the model can produce, so the reply always parses and always has the required fields. Tool calling with a JSON schema for the arguments works in a similar way, though some setups treat the schema as a strong hint rather than a hard rule. Validation is still needed, because a schema guarantees the shape and not the content. A total of -40 or a date in 2087 is valid JSON. When a check fails, retry with the error message included, and after a few failures send the invoice to a human queue.

A stronger prompt lowers the failure rate but guarantees nothing, and a regex that grabs the first brace block breaks on nested objects and happily accepts a reply with a missing field. Temperature 0 makes output less random, but the most likely token sequence can still be malformed, and every invoice is a new input anyway. A second LLM call to convert text into JSON adds cost and latency and has exactly the same failure mode as the first call.
questions.deeper: In an interview, separate three layers: format (does it parse), schema (are the right fields there with the right types) and business rules (does the total equal the sum of line items). Constrained decoding handles the first two. Only your own code handles the third.

questions.prompt:
Using NumPy 2.x, each of 32 query embeddings is compared with each of 10 cluster centroids. What is the shape of `d`? Write it as a Python tuple.

```python
import numpy as np
queries = np.zeros((32, 1, 64))
centroids = np.zeros((10, 64))
d = queries - centroids
```
questions.explanation:
NumPy broadcasting lines the shapes up from the right and compares one dimension at a time. Two sizes fit together if they are equal or one of them is 1. A missing dimension counts as 1.

```text
queries:   (32,  1, 64)
centroids: (     10, 64)
result:    (32, 10, 64)
```

The last dimensions are both 64. In the middle, the 1 stretches to match 10. On the left, `centroids` has no dimension, so it is treated as 1 and stretched to 32. The result holds every query minus every centroid, the first step of a distance matrix.

The common mistake is to line the shapes up from the left. That pairs 32 with 10 and suggests the code fails. Another slip is to expect (32, 64), as if each query met only one centroid. The extra axis of size 1 in `queries` is exactly what makes the pairwise result possible.
questions.deeper: Interviewers often follow up with memory. Here the result holds 32 × 10 × 64 = 20,480 floats, which is fine. With a million queries and 10,000 centroids it would be far too large, so real code uses ‖a − b‖² = ‖a‖² − 2a·b + ‖b‖², which needs one matrix multiply and no 3D array.

questions.prompt: You want to run a 7-billion-parameter model on a laptop GPU after quantizing its weights to 4 bits each. How much memory do the weights alone need? Ignore any extra storage for quantization scales. Give the answer in GB, where 1 GB = 10⁹ bytes, to 1 decimal place.
questions.explanation:
Memory for weights is the number of parameters times the bytes per parameter. A byte has 8 bits, so 4 bits is 0.5 bytes. That gives 7 × 10⁹ × 0.5 = 3.5 × 10⁹ bytes, which is 3.5 GB.

The most common mistake is to treat 4 bits as 4 bytes, which gives 28 GB, the size of the model in fp32. A quick table helps: fp32 uses 4 bytes per parameter (28 GB here), fp16 and bf16 use 2 bytes (14 GB), int8 uses 1 byte (7 GB) and 4-bit uses half a byte (3.5 GB). In practice, 4-bit formats also store a scale for each small group of weights, so the real file is a little larger than 3.5 GB, which is why the prompt says to ignore it.
questions.deeper: Weights are only part of the memory story at inference time. A strong candidate adds the KV cache, which grows with context length and batch size, plus activations and framework overhead. A model whose weights barely fit will often run out of memory once real traffic with long prompts arrives.

questions.prompt: Three AI applications run inside one company: a chat assistant, a coding assistant and an analytics bot. Each one has its own hand-written connectors for GitHub, the ticketing system and the data warehouse, which makes nine connectors in all. An engineer proposes adopting the Model Context Protocol (MCP). What does MCP give them?
options: A shared standard, so each system is wrapped once as an MCP server that any MCP-capable application can use.
A fine-tuning method that teaches each model the three systems' APIs, so the applications no longer need tool calls.
A much larger context window, so each application can load all three systems' contents into its prompt.
A security layer that makes every tool call safe, so the servers no longer need any access controls of their own.
questions.explanation:
MCP is an open standard for connecting AI applications to tools and data. A system such as GitHub is wrapped once as an MCP server, which describes its tools and data in a common format. Any application that speaks MCP can connect to that server as a client. With three applications and three systems, the team goes from nine custom connectors to three servers, and a fourth application gets all three systems without new connector code. It works like a shared plug standard.

MCP is not training. The model still calls tools at run time, and MCP only standardizes how those tools are described and invoked. It does not change the context window either, since it is about connections, not memory. It is also not a security layer. An MCP server can be over-privileged, buggy or even malicious, and its tool descriptions can carry prompt injection. You still need authentication, least-privilege access and a review of any third-party server before trusting it.
questions.deeper: A good follow-up answer explains the roles: the host application runs one client per server connection, and servers expose tools (actions), resources (data to read) and prompts (reusable templates). Strong candidates also point out the supply-chain risk of installing community servers without review.

questions.prompt: A bank's loan default model has been live for a year. Monitoring shows the mix of applicants looks the same as in training: income, debt ratio and age have barely moved. But applicants with a given profile now default more often than the model predicts. What best describes this change?
options: Concept drift: the same inputs now lead to different outcomes, so P(y | x) has changed.
Data drift: the inputs have moved away from the training data, so P(x) is now different.
Training-serving skew: production computes the features differently from the training pipeline.
Overfitting: the model memorised its training set, and this only shows up after months live.
questions.explanation:
The clue is that the inputs look the same, but the outcome for the same inputs has changed. That is concept drift. The relationship the model learned, the chance of default given a profile, is no longer true. A recession or a change in lending rules can do this without changing who applies.

Data drift, also called covariate shift, means P(x) moves, for example a sudden wave of younger applicants. Monitoring says the inputs have barely moved, so that does not fit. Training-serving skew is a pipeline bug where features are built differently in production. It usually shows up as odd feature values from the first day, not as a gradual rise in defaults for the same profiles. Overfitting shows up as a gap between training and held-out scores before launch. It does not explain a model that was fine for months and then got worse.
questions.deeper: Concept drift is the harder kind to catch, because input monitoring cannot see it. You need labels, or a fast proxy for them, to notice. A strong answer adds that the usual fix is retraining on recent data, sometimes with more weight on recent rows, and checking whether the features still capture what drives the outcome.

questions.prompt: A team fits a scaler and a mean imputer on the whole dataset, then splits it into train and test sets. The test score comes out a little too optimistic, because statistics from the test rows shaped the training features. This problem is called data ______.
questions.explanation:
Leakage means information the model should not have at training time gets into training. Here the scaler's mean and standard deviation, and the imputer's fill values, were computed using the test rows. So the training features already carry a little knowledge of the test set, and the test score no longer measures performance on truly unseen data.

The common wrong answer is overfitting. Overfitting is when a model learns noise in its own training data. It shows up as a gap between training and test scores. Leakage is different: it makes the test score itself untrustworthy, often with no visible gap. The fix is to split first, then fit every preprocessing step on the training rows only. In scikit-learn, putting the scaler and imputer inside a `Pipeline` means cross-validation refits them on each training fold automatically.
questions.deeper: With a simple scaler on a large dataset, the effect is often small. It gets serious with steps that look at the target, such as target encoding or feature selection on the full data. Interviewers often ask you to name such a step and explain how a pipeline prevents it.

questions.prompt: A credit team wants to tell each applicant which features pushed their score up or down. They use a method borrowed from cooperative game theory. It treats features as players, averages each feature's contribution over every order in which features could be added, and makes the contributions add up to the gap between that prediction and the average prediction. The method is usually called ______.
questions.explanation:
SHAP, short for Shapley additive explanations, rests on the Shapley value from game theory. The payout is the prediction, and a fair share for each player is its average extra contribution over every order of joining. Answering "Shapley values" is also accepted, since that is the quantity SHAP computes. The property that suits a credit letter is additivity: the base value, the model's average output, plus all the feature contributions equals this applicant's prediction. So the explanation reads as a list of pushes up and down that sum exactly.

The common wrong answer is LIME. LIME also explains single predictions, but it does so by fitting a simple local model to perturbed samples. It does not use Shapley values and its contributions are not guaranteed to add up to the prediction. Another slip is permutation importance, which ranks features for the whole model rather than explaining one prediction.
questions.deeper: Exact Shapley values are costly, so TreeSHAP is used for tree models and sampling methods for others. A good interview point: SHAP explains the model, not the world. Correlated features can share or swap credit, so a SHAP value is not a causal effect.

questions.prompt:
Using pandas 3.x, what value does `out` hold after this code runs? Give it as a decimal to 2 places.

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "store": ["a", "a", "b", "b", "b"],
    "sales": [10.0, np.nan, 30.0, np.nan, 60.0],
})
df["sales"] = df["sales"].fillna(df["sales"].mean())
out = df.groupby("store")["sales"].mean()["b"]
```
questions.explanation:
Work through it in two steps.

Step 1: `df["sales"].mean()` skips NaN by default. It averages 10, 30 and 60, which is 100 / 3 ≈ 33.33. Both missing values become 33.33.

Step 2: store b now holds 30, 33.33 and 60. Their mean is 123.33 / 3 ≈ 41.11.

The most common mistake is to think the mean treats NaN as zero, giving 100 / 5 = 20 as the fill value and (30 + 20 + 60) / 3 ≈ 36.67 for store b. Another is to skip the fill in your head and average store b's real values only, (30 + 60) / 2 = 45. Note that the fill uses the global mean, not each store's own mean. Filling by store would need `groupby("store")["sales"].transform("mean")` instead.
questions.deeper: Filling with a mean pulls group averages toward the global average and shrinks variance, which can hide real differences between stores. In an interview, mention adding a was-missing flag column and computing fill values from training data only, so the fill does not leak test information.

questions.subtopic: bias and variance from learning curves
questions.prompt: A gradient-boosted model predicts which parcels will arrive late. On the full training set its training error is 3% and its validation error is 17%. Experienced dispatchers make about 4% errors on the same task. What does this pattern show?
options: High variance: it fits the training data closely but fails to generalize, so it is overfitting.
High bias: the model is too simple to capture the real pattern in the data, so it is underfitting.
A good fit: the training error is already below the human level, so the model has learned the task.
High bias and high variance together, because validation error sits far above the human level.
questions.explanation:
Read the two gaps separately. The gap between training error and the human-level error tells you about bias. Here training error (3%) is at or below what dispatchers achieve (4%), so the model is flexible enough and bias is low. The gap between training and validation error tells you about variance. Here it is 14 points, which is large. Low bias plus a big train to validation gap means the model has memorised the training data and is overfitting.

The high bias reading would need training error itself to be high, well above 4%. Calling it a good fit ignores the validation number, which is the one that predicts real performance. The option claiming both problems at once mixes up the two gaps. Validation error is far above human level only because of the variance gap, since training error shows no bias problem.
questions.deeper: A strong answer names the next steps for high variance: more data, stronger regularization, shallower trees or fewer boosting rounds, and early stopping. An interviewer may then ask what you would do if training error were 15% instead. That flips the diagnosis to bias, and the fix becomes a richer model or better features.

questions.prompt: A credit model's score is split into 5 bins. At training time the share of applicants in each bin was 0.10, 0.20, 0.40, 0.20 and 0.10. This month the shares are 0.05, 0.15, 0.35, 0.25 and 0.20. Compute the population stability index (PSI) using the natural log. Give it as a decimal to 3 places.
questions.explanation:
PSI adds one term per bin: (actual − expected) × ln(actual / expected). Every term is positive when the share moved, in either direction, because the difference and the log always have the same sign.

- Bin 1: (0.05 − 0.10) × ln(0.5) = −0.05 × −0.693 = 0.0347
- Bin 2: (0.15 − 0.20) × ln(0.75) = −0.05 × −0.288 = 0.0144
- Bin 3: (0.35 − 0.40) × ln(0.875) = −0.05 × −0.134 = 0.0067
- Bin 4: (0.25 − 0.20) × ln(1.25) = 0.05 × 0.223 = 0.0112
- Bin 5: (0.20 − 0.10) × ln(2) = 0.10 × 0.693 = 0.0693

The sum is 0.136.

Two mistakes are common. Using log base 10 gives 0.059, which would wrongly read as no drift. Computing only Σ actual × ln(actual / expected) gives 0.070. That is the KL divergence in one direction. PSI is the symmetric version, the sum of the KL divergence taken in both directions.
questions.deeper: A common rule of thumb reads PSI below 0.1 as stable, 0.1 to 0.25 as a moderate shift worth a look, and above 0.25 as a major shift. At 0.136 this deserves a look, and half of it comes from the top bin doubling. Watch for empty bins: a share of zero breaks the log, so teams add a small floor such as 0.0001.

questions.prompt: A mobile app runs an image classifier on the phone. Post-training quantization to int8 cost a small, acceptable drop in accuracy. Pushing the same method to 4-bit weights causes a large drop. You still have the training code and data. Which of these steps is most likely to win back most of the lost accuracy?
options: Use quantization-aware training, which simulates the 4-bit rounding in the forward pass while training, so the weights adapt to it and much of the accuracy returns.
Switch to dynamic quantization, which computes activation scales on the fly for each input image, so every image gets scales that fit it and the 4-bit error goes away.
Rerun post-training quantization with a much larger calibration set of training images, so the value ranges are estimated better and the 4-bit rounding error mostly disappears.
Also quantize the activations to 4 bits, since the large drop comes from mixing 4-bit weights with higher-precision activations inside the same layers of the network.
questions.explanation:
Post-training quantization rounds the weights of a model that was trained in full precision and never had to cope with rounding. At int8 the rounding steps are small, so the damage is small. At 4 bits there are only 16 levels, and the errors add up across layers. Quantization-aware training inserts simulated quantization into the forward pass and keeps training, passing gradients straight through the rounding, so the network adjusts its weights to work well at low precision. It costs extra training time but usually recovers much of the gap.

Dynamic quantization only computes activation scales on the fly for each input. The weights are still rounded to the same 16 levels, so their error stays. A bigger calibration set gives slightly better value ranges, but calibration only sets ranges. It cannot restore the information lost when trained weights are rounded to 16 levels, which is why int8 was fine and 4 bits was not. Quantizing activations to 4 bits adds more rounding error, which makes accuracy worse, not better. Keeping the most sensitive layers at higher precision is another sound fix, but it is not among the options.
questions.deeper: In interviews, mention the cheaper options to try before full quantization-aware training: stronger post-training methods that minimize each layer's output error, keeping sensitive layers such as the first and last at higher precision, and per-channel scales. Always measure accuracy on slices, since quantization damage is often uneven across classes.

questions.prompt: A payments team has millions of card transactions but no fraud labels yet. They want to flag unusual transactions for review. Which methods can do this without labels? Select all that apply.
options: Isolation forest, flagging points that are split off in few steps
Local outlier factor, flagging points in much sparser areas than their neighbours
An autoencoder, flagging transactions with high reconstruction error
Logistic regression with class weights, trained to predict the fraud flag
SMOTE oversampling of the fraud class, followed by a random forest
A t-test comparing the amounts of fraud and genuine transactions
questions.explanation:
All three keys learn what normal looks like from the data alone and score how far each point is from it.

An isolation forest builds random trees that split on random features and values. Odd points sit far from the crowd, so they get isolated in only a few splits, and a short average path means a high anomaly score. Local outlier factor compares how dense the area around a point is with the density around its neighbours, which catches points that are unusual locally. An autoencoder learns to compress and rebuild transactions. Since most traffic is normal, it rebuilds normal patterns well and rare ones badly, so high reconstruction error flags them.

The other three all need a fraud label. Logistic regression has nothing to predict without one. SMOTE creates synthetic examples of a labelled minority class, so it cannot run when no rows are marked as fraud. A t-test compares two labelled groups and is a test, not a way to score single transactions.
questions.deeper: In production these scores feed an analyst queue, and the analysts' decisions become the first labels. A strong candidate explains the move from unsupervised scoring to a supervised model once enough labels exist, and warns that unusual is not the same as fraud. Big but legitimate purchases will also look odd.

questions.prompt: A screening test for a liver condition is used on a population where 0.5% of people have the condition. The test catches 95% of people who have it (sensitivity) and gives a positive result for 3% of people who do not (false positive rate). A person tests positive. What is the probability they have the condition? Give it as a decimal to 2 places.
questions.explanation:
Bayes theorem says P(condition | positive) = P(positive | condition) × P(condition) / P(positive).

It helps to picture 100,000 people. 500 have the condition, and the test catches 95% of them, so 475 true positives. 99,500 do not have it, and 3% of them test positive, so 2,985 false positives. In total 475 + 2,985 = 3,460 people test positive, and 475 / 3,460 ≈ 0.137, which rounds to 0.14.

The common mistake is to answer 0.95, mixing up P(positive | condition) with P(condition | positive). Another is to forget that the false positive rate applies to the huge healthy group. Even a small 3% of 99,500 people outnumbers all the true cases six to one. That is why a positive screen for a rare condition is usually followed by a second, more specific test.
questions.deeper: The same base-rate effect drives alert fatigue in fraud and security systems. A model with 95% recall and a 3% false alarm rate still produces mostly false alerts when the event is rare. A strong candidate reaches for precision, or positive predictive value, and shows how it changes as prevalence changes.

questions.prompt: A news app has 20 million daily active users. Each user opens the feed 5 times a day on average, and each open sends 2 requests to the recommendation service. Peak-hour traffic is 3 times the daily average rate. Using 86,400 seconds in a day, what peak load in requests per second must the service handle? Give a whole number.
questions.explanation:
Work out the daily total, turn it into a per-second average, then scale up to the peak.

- Requests per day: 20,000,000 × 5 × 2 = 200,000,000
- Average rate: 200,000,000 / 86,400 ≈ 2,314.8 requests per second
- Peak rate: 2,314.8 × 3 ≈ 6,944 requests per second

The most common mistake is to stop at the average, about 2,315. A service sized for the average falls over every evening, because traffic bunches into busy hours. Another slip is to forget the 2 requests per open, which gives about 3,472. In a live interview, rounding a day to 100,000 seconds is fine for speed and gives about 6,000, but this question fixes 86,400 so there is one exact answer.
questions.deeper: After the peak, interviewers ask what it means for hardware. If one replica of the ranking model handles 500 requests per second within the latency target, you need about 14 replicas at peak, plus 30 to 50% headroom for spikes and a failed node. Caching popular feeds can cut the load further.

questions.prompt:
A teammate evaluates a churn model with this scikit-learn code. What is wrong, and what is the best fix?

```python
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score

X_scaled = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)
scores = cross_val_score(LogisticRegression(), X_scaled, y, cv=5)
```
options: The scaler is fit on all rows, held-out folds included. Wrap the scaler and model in a Pipeline and cross-validate that.
Nothing leaks, because the scaler never looks at `y`. The scores are a fair estimate of new data, so the code can stay as it is.
The scaler should be refit on each validation fold inside the loop, so that every fold is scaled by its own mean and variance.
The folds are not stratified, so class balance varies between them. Pass `cv=StratifiedKFold(5)` to keep the scaling consistent.
questions.explanation:
`fit_transform(X)` computes the mean and standard deviation from all rows before cross-validation starts. So in every fold, the validation rows have already shaped the scaling of the training rows, and the model gets a small peek at data it is later scored on. With a Pipeline, `cross_val_score` refits the scaler on the four training folds each time and only applies it to the held-out fold. That matches production, where the scaler never sees future data.

The claim that nothing leaks because the scaler never sees `y` is the trap. Leakage is any information from the evaluation data reaching training, labels or not. With a plain scaler the effect is often small, but the same habit with imputers, target encoders or feature selection can inflate scores a lot. Refitting on each validation fold is wrong the other way: held-out rows should be transformed with training statistics, never used to fit. Stratification is not the problem either. For a classifier, `cv=5` already uses stratified folds, and it says nothing about where the scaler was fit.
questions.deeper: Interviewers like to ask which steps belong inside the Pipeline. The answer is anything that learns from data: scalers, imputers, encoders and feature selectors. A good habit is to make the Pipeline the object you tune with GridSearchCV, so every candidate in the search is scored without leakage.

questions.prompt: Inside each transformer block, every token's activation vector is normalized on its own: subtract the mean of that vector's features, divide by their standard deviation, then apply a learned scale and shift. No statistics are shared across the examples in a batch. This normalization is called ______.
questions.explanation:
Layer normalization computes the mean and standard deviation over the features of a single token's vector, so each token is normalized independently of every other token and every other example. That makes it behave the same at any batch size and any sequence length, in training and at inference.

The common wrong answer is batch normalization. Batch norm computes statistics for each feature across the examples in a batch and keeps running averages for use at inference. That fits transformers poorly. Sequences have different lengths, and padding tokens would pollute the batch statistics. Batches of long sequences are often small, so the estimates are noisy. During generation the model processes one new token at a time, where batch statistics make little sense, and running averages from training may not match what the model sees in production. RMSNorm is also ruled out, since it skips the mean subtraction and the shift that the prompt describes.
questions.deeper: Many recent LLMs use RMSNorm, a lighter variant that skips the mean subtraction and the shift and only divides by the root mean square. A likely follow-up is pre-norm versus post-norm: placing the normalization before each sublayer, as most modern models do, makes deep transformers train more stably.

questions.prompt: A fine-tuning method keeps a pretrained weight matrix W frozen and unquantized at its original precision, and learns an update ΔW = BA, where B and A are thin matrices of rank r, much smaller than the dimensions of W. Only A and B are trained. This method is called ______.
questions.explanation:
LoRA, short for low-rank adaptation, assumes the change needed to adapt a model to a new task has low rank. Instead of updating W directly, it trains two thin matrices whose product BA has the same shape as W. For a 4,096 × 4,096 layer, full fine-tuning updates about 16.8 million weights. With r = 8, B is 4,096 × 8 and A is 8 × 4,096, which is 65,536 weights, about 0.4% of the layer. After training, BA can be merged into W, so inference costs nothing extra.

A common mix-up is with QLoRA, which uses the same low-rank update but stores the frozen base model in 4-bit precision. The prompt says the base stays unquantized at its original precision, which rules it out. Adapters and prefix tuning are also parameter-efficient, but they add new layers or tokens rather than a low-rank update to existing weights.
questions.deeper: Interviewers often ask which layers to apply LoRA to and how to pick the rank. A strong answer mentions the attention projections as a common start, trying a few ranks on a validation set, and the serving benefit: one base model can host many small task adapters and swap them per request.

questions.prompt: An HR assistant answers employee questions from a 300-page policy handbook. The handbook is split into 1,500-token chunks with no overlap, and each chunk usually spans several policy sections. For narrow questions such as "How many days of bereavement leave do I get?", the chunk that holds the answer often ranks below chunks about unrelated policies. Which change is most likely to help?
options: Split on section headings into chunks of a few hundred tokens, with a small overlap, so each covers one topic.
Merge chunks to about 4,000 tokens, so each embedding carries the full context of every policy that the chunk touches.
Keep the 1,500-token size but add 50% overlap between neighbours, so no answer sentence is ever cut in half.
Keep the 1,500-token chunks and prepend the handbook title to each one, so every embedding knows its source.
questions.explanation:
Each chunk becomes one embedding vector, which acts like a summary of everything in the chunk. When one chunk covers leave, expenses and travel, its vector lands somewhere between those topics, so a narrow question about bereavement leave matches it only weakly. Smaller chunks cut along the handbook's own structure give focused vectors that a narrow query can match strongly. A small overlap keeps a sentence that straddles a boundary readable in at least one chunk.

There is a limit in the other direction. Chunks that are too small lose their context, such as a line saying "This also applies to contractors" without the policy it refers to. That is why a few hundred tokens split on headings is a common middle ground.

Merging into larger chunks makes the dilution worse and also fills the model's prompt with unrelated text. Heavy overlap fixes sentences being cut at boundaries, which is not the problem described, and roughly doubles the index size. Prepending a title is a useful trick when chunks come from many documents, but here every chunk gets the same title, so it adds identical words to every vector and does nothing to separate topics.
questions.deeper: A strong answer says chunk size is a tuning knob you measure, not guess. Build a small set of real questions with known answer passages, then compare recall@k for a few chunk sizes. Many teams also store the section heading with each chunk and return the parent section to the model once a small chunk matches.

questions.subtopic: choosing a threshold from business costs
questions.prompt: A telecom company has a churn model that outputs a probability for each customer. The retention team can make at most 300 calls a week. Each call costs $15. A churner who gets a call stays 25% of the time, and a customer who stays is worth $400. Calling a customer who was not going to churn gains nothing. How would you choose the score threshold for who gets a call?
questions.answer: I would set the threshold from expected value, not from 0.5. A call to a customer with churn probability p is worth p × 0.25 × $400 = $100p and costs $15, so it pays off when p is above 0.15. That is the break-even threshold. Capacity also binds. If more than 300 customers score above 0.15, I would call the 300 highest scores, so the real threshold becomes the 300th score. If fewer clear 0.15, I would call only those and leave spare capacity unused. This only works if the probabilities are calibrated, so I would check a reliability plot first. Then I would confirm the value with a holdout group that gets no calls, and revisit the threshold when costs, save rates or the score distribution change.
points: Compare the cost of a wasted call with the value lost from a missed churner
Break-even probability is cost divided by value times save rate, here 0.15
The 300-call cap means taking the top 300 scores when many clear break-even
Scores must be calibrated for the break-even rule to hold
Validate with a no-call holdout and update the threshold as inputs change
questions.explanation:
The threshold is a business decision, so it should come from what each mistake costs. A false positive wastes a $15 call. A missed churner who could have been saved loses the expected value of the call, which is 0.25 × $400 = $100 for a sure churner. Setting p × 100 = 15 gives p = 0.15. Above that, a call is worth more than it costs on average.

The common mistake is to keep the default 0.5 or to pick the threshold that maximises F1. Both ignore the costs. Here 0.5 would skip many customers who are worth calling. The second mistake is to forget the capacity cap. When demand exceeds 300 calls, you rank by score and stop at 300, and the cap, not the break-even point, sets the cut. Finally, the break-even rule assumes a score of 0.2 really means a 20% chance of churn. An uncalibrated model breaks that link.
questions.deeper: A strong candidate notes that the 25% save rate is not the same for everyone. Some customers would stay anyway and some cannot be saved. Uplift modelling targets the customers whose behaviour the call actually changes, which often beats ranking by churn risk alone.

questions.prompt: Suppose a data-cleaning agent completes a job in 20 steps, one after another. Each step succeeds with probability 0.97, independently of the others, and the job fails if any single step fails. What percentage of jobs succeed end to end? Give the answer as a percentage to 1 decimal place.
questions.explanation:
The job succeeds only if all 20 steps succeed. Because the steps are independent, you multiply their success probabilities: 0.97 raised to the power 20.

- 0.97² = 0.9409
- 0.97⁴ = 0.9409² ≈ 0.8853
- 0.97⁵ ≈ 0.8853 × 0.97 ≈ 0.8587
- 0.97¹⁰ ≈ 0.8587² ≈ 0.7374
- 0.97²⁰ ≈ 0.7374² ≈ 0.5438, which is 54.4%

The most common mistake is to feel that 97% per step is "high" and expect most jobs to pass. Almost half fail. A second mistake is to subtract the error rates linearly: 20 × 3% = 60% failure, giving 40% success. That shortcut only works when the total error is small. For larger totals it overcounts, because once a job has failed, a second failure in the same job does not fail it again.

The same maths shows why small per-step gains matter so much. At 0.99 per step, 20 steps give about 81.8% success.
questions.deeper: Interviewers may turn it around: what per-step rate gives 90% over 20 steps? The answer is 0.9^(1/20) ≈ 0.995. In practice agents beat this simple product by checking their own work and retrying failed steps, which breaks the assumption that one failure ends the job.

questions.prompt: A bank's loan model approves 30% of applicants in group X and 30% of applicants in group Y. Among applicants who would actually repay, it approves 60% in group X but only 40% in group Y. Which statement is correct?
options: It meets demographic parity but fails equal opportunity, since true repayers are approved at unequal rates.
It meets equal opportunity, since applicants in both groups are approved at the same overall rate of 30%.
It meets both criteria, since equal approval rates also mean equal approval rates among those who would repay.
It fails demographic parity, since applicants who would repay are approved at a higher rate in group X.
questions.explanation:
Demographic parity asks only whether each group is approved at the same overall rate. Both groups get 30%, so it holds. Equal opportunity asks whether people who truly deserve a yes, here those who would repay, get one at the same rate. That is the true positive rate, 60% against 40%, so it fails.

The option claiming equal opportunity holds uses the overall rate, which is the parity test, not the opportunity test. The option claiming both hold assumes equal approval rates force equal true positive rates. They do not, because the groups can differ in how many applicants would repay and in how many non-repayers get approved. The option claiming parity fails applies the opportunity test to the parity criterion.

The two goals can pull against each other. When repayment rates differ between groups, equal approval rates usually push true positive rates apart. Getting both at once generally means accepting different false positive rates per group.
questions.deeper: There is no single fair metric. In an interview, say which harm matters for the use case. In lending, qualified applicants being refused points toward equal opportunity. Then say who should decide the trade-off: legal, policy and affected groups, not only the ML team.

questions.prompt:
A colleague's PyTorch training loop for a demand-forecasting model looks like this:

```python
optimizer = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.01)
for x, y in loader:
    pred = model(x)
    loss = loss_fn(pred, y)
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()
```

What goes wrong when it runs?
options: Each `backward()` call adds to the stored gradients, so every step uses the sum of all past batch gradients, not just the current batch's gradient.
PyTorch clears the stored gradients inside `optimizer.step()`, so this loop trains exactly like one that calls `zero_grad()` on every iteration.
Each `backward()` call replaces the gradients from the previous batch, so the loop trains correctly and the missing reset only wastes a little memory.
The first `optimizer.step()` call raises a RuntimeError, because PyTorch will not apply gradients that were not zeroed before `backward()` ran.
questions.explanation:
In PyTorch, `loss.backward()` adds the new gradients into each parameter's `.grad` field rather than replacing what is there. Nothing in this loop clears that field, so after batch 50 the update uses the sum of all 50 batch gradients, each computed at older weights. The steps end up far larger than intended, and the loss usually oscillates or diverges. The fix is to call `optimizer.zero_grad()` once per iteration, before `loss.backward()`.

The option claiming the optimizer step clears gradients is a common belief, but the step only reads `.grad` and updates the weights. The option about replacing gradients describes how many people expect autograd to work, and it is exactly the wrong way round. No error is raised either. PyTorch accumulates on purpose, because that behaviour is what makes gradient accumulation across micro-batches possible.
questions.deeper: A strong candidate mentions the intended use of accumulation: run several micro-batches, call `backward()` on each loss divided by the number of micro-batches, then step and zero once. That simulates a larger batch on limited memory. Interviewers may also ask where `zero_grad()` belongs, and any point before the next `backward()` works.

questions.prompt: A team is tuning text generation for a product-description writer. Which statements about decoding settings are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Greedy decoding picks the most likely next token at every step, so it involves no random sampling.
A temperature above 1 flattens the next-token distribution, so less likely tokens are chosen more often.
Top-p sampling with p = 0.9 samples from the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities add up to at least 0.9.
Lowering the temperature toward 0 makes the output more varied, because it removes the bias toward common tokens.
Top-p sampling keeps the same number of candidate tokens at every step, however peaked the distribution is.
Greedy decoding is guaranteed to return the most likely complete sequence for the given prompt.
questions.explanation:
Greedy decoding takes the highest-probability token at each step, so it has no sampling randomness, and the same input gives the same output apart from small numerical effects on some hardware. Temperature divides the logits before the softmax. A value above 1 shrinks the gaps between logits and flattens the distribution, so unlikely tokens get picked more often and the text becomes more varied. Top-p, or nucleus, sampling sorts tokens by probability, keeps the smallest set whose total reaches p, and samples from that set.

Lowering the temperature does the opposite of what the false statement claims. It sharpens the distribution, and as it nears 0 sampling approaches greedy decoding, so output becomes less varied. Keeping a fixed number of candidates describes top-k. Top-p adapts: when the model is confident, a few tokens reach 0.9, and when it is unsure, many tokens are needed. Greedy is only best one step at a time. A slightly less likely first token can lead to a much more likely full sequence, which is why beam search exists.
questions.deeper: For product descriptions, a strong answer picks settings per field: greedy or a low temperature where facts such as sizes and materials must be exact and consistent, and a moderate temperature with top-p for the creative copy. Interviewers often follow up on why greedy text can become repetitive and how repetition penalties help.

questions.prompt: A grocery chain forecasts daily sales per store from three years of history. Features include sales lags and 7-day rolling averages. Shuffled 5-fold cross-validation gave an error of 6%, but the first month in production showed 14%. Which change to the validation setup best fixes the misleading estimate?
options: Use forward-chaining splits that train on earlier dates and validate on the dates right after.
Use stratified 5-fold so that each fold holds the same mix of high-sales and low-sales days.
Move to 10 folds so each validation fold is smaller and the error estimate becomes less noisy.
Keep the shuffled folds but fit feature scaling on each training fold only, never on validation rows.
questions.explanation:
Shuffling puts days from after a validation day into the training set. With lag and rolling features, neighbouring days share almost the same information, so the model is really filling in gaps between days it has already seen. That is much easier than forecasting the future, which is what production asks for. Forward-chaining splits (sometimes called rolling-origin or time series split) train only on the past and test on the period right after, so the validation task matches the real one.

Stratifying by sales level still shuffles across time, so the leak stays. More folds changes how noisy the estimate is, not the fact that each fold peeks at the future. Fitting the scaler on the training fold only fixes a real but much smaller leak. It does nothing about the model training on days that come after the days it is tested on.
questions.deeper: A strong candidate adds a gap between train and validation windows when features look back several days, so rolling averages near the boundary cannot see validation rows. They also make the validation horizon match production, for example a 14-day forecast window if the business plans two weeks ahead.

questions.prompt: Fine-tuning a vision model on one GPU at a batch size of 64 fails with an out-of-memory error. Which of these changes reduce peak GPU memory during training? Select all that apply.
options: Mixed-precision training, which keeps most activations in 16-bit rather than 32-bit floats
Gradient checkpointing, which keeps only some activations in the forward pass and recomputes the rest during backward
