Uplift modelling targets those whose decision a call can change, and a holdout group that receives no calls is how you measure whether the programme works at all.

questions.prompt: A lender trained a default model after downsampling non-default loans to balance the classes. On a holdout set with the natural default rate, ROC-AUC is 0.91. Among the 1,200 holdout loans the model scored between 0.8 and 0.9, only 40% defaulted. The pricing team wants to use the scores as default probabilities. What should you conclude?
options: Ranking is strong but the scores overstate risk, so fit a calibration map on natural-rate data before pricing.
An AUC of 0.91 shows the scores are reliable probabilities, so the 40% default rate in that band is likely sampling noise.
Recalibrating will also lift AUC well above 0.91, because AUC penalises probabilities that are badly scaled.
Retrain with even heavier downsampling, so the model sees enough defaults to produce calibrated probabilities.
questions.explanation:
Calibration means that among loans scored about 0.85, about 85% default. Here only 40% did, so the scores are far too high. AUC cannot catch this. It only checks whether defaulters are ranked above non-defaulters, and any order-preserving change to the scores leaves it the same. So a model can rank very well and still give badly wrong probabilities. The fix is to fit a calibration map, such as Platt scaling or isotonic regression, on held-out data that has the real default rate.

The noise option fails on sample size. With 1,200 loans, the standard error of a 40% rate is about 1.4 points, tiny next to a gap of at least 40 points. The option about lifting AUC is backwards: calibration keeps the ranking, so AUC stays about the same. Heavier downsampling makes things worse. Removing more non-defaults raises the default rate the model sees in training, which pushes its scores up even further.
questions.deeper: Downsampling is a common cause of this, and there is a known prior-correction formula that maps scores back to the true base rate. Interviewers like candidates who check a reliability diagram or expected calibration error before anyone multiplies a score by a loan amount.

questions.subtopic: validation looked good, production did not
questions.prompt: A loan default model scored 0.91 ROC-AUC on a held-out validation set. One month after launch, measured on real applications, its ROC-AUC is 0.68. List the most likely causes and how you would check each one.
questions.answer: First I would look for leakage. A feature such as number of collection calls or account status may only be filled in after a default, so it is present in historical rows but not at decision time. I would list each feature with the time it becomes known. Second, the split. If one customer appears in both train and validation, or rows were shuffled across time, validation was too easy. I would re-score on a strict out-of-time split. Third, overuse of the validation set. Many rounds of tuning against it inflate its score, so I would check a fresh holdout. Fourth, shift. A new marketing channel or a policy change may bring different applicants, which I would see by comparing feature distributions. Fifth, train-serving skew, where the live pipeline computes features differently. Last, after one month most loans have not had time to default, so the production labels may be immature.
points: Leakage from features only known after the outcome
Wrong split, such as random rows or the same customer in both sets
Validation set overused during tuning
Distribution shift in the applicant population
Train-serving skew in feature computation
Immature labels one month after launch
questions.explanation:
A drop from 0.91 to 0.68 is too large to be noise, so something made the validation number unrealistic or the live setting different. Leakage is the first suspect because it inflates validation in exactly this way. The test is simple: for every feature, ask whether it would exist at the moment the loan is decided. A random split is the next suspect, because it lets the model see the same people, or the future, during training.

The most common mistake is to jump straight to drift and retrain on newer data. If the cause is leakage or skew, retraining reproduces the same bug. Another miss is the label itself. Default takes months to happen, so after one month the live labels mostly show early defaults, which behave differently from the full set. Comparing like with like, using the same label window in both places, is part of a fair diagnosis.
questions.deeper: A strong candidate proposes a replay test: score last quarter's applications through the live feature pipeline and compare with the offline features row by row. Mismatches point to skew, and a gap that remains on matched features points to leakage or shift. Interviewers like candidates who check cheap explanations before retraining anything.

questions.prompt: Your team built an IT helpdesk agent. It reads a ticket, then uses tools to look up the user, reset passwords, unlock accounts and install approved software. Before rollout, the head of IT asks how you will know it works and is safe. Design the evaluation.
questions.answer: I would run the agent in a sandbox with fake users, accounts and software, so it can act without touching production. I would build a few hundred test tickets from real history, each with the correct end state, such as the account unlocked and nothing else changed. Task success is judged by checking that final state, not the agent's own claim. I would also check the trajectory: did it pick the right tools, pass valid arguments and avoid needless or repeated calls. I would track steps, cost and latency per ticket. Safety cases matter most: requests for unapproved software, a user asking to reset someone else's password, and tickets carrying injected instructions. Since agents are not deterministic, I would run each ticket several times and report the pass rate. Humans would review a sample of traces, and the whole suite would run again on every change.
points: Sandbox with fake accounts, success judged by the final state
Trajectory checks: right tools, valid arguments, no needless calls
Steps, cost and latency per task
Safety and adversarial cases, including prompt injection and permission abuse
Repeated runs to measure consistency
Human review of traces and a regression suite on every change
questions.explanation:
An agent changes things in the world, so the evaluation has to look at what it did, not only at what it said. The most common mistake is to grade the agent's final message. An agent can report "password reset done" after calling the wrong tool, or after resetting the wrong account. Checking the actual end state in a sandbox catches that, and checking that nothing else changed catches side effects.

A second mistake is to look only at success rate. Two agents can both solve 90% of tickets while one takes 4 steps and the other takes 30, with very different cost and risk. Trajectory checks show this, and they also expose unsafe paths that happen to end well. Safety cases need their own set, because normal tickets rarely test whether the agent refuses a request it should refuse. Finally, agents vary from run to run. A ticket that passes once may fail on the next run, so measure the pass rate over repeated attempts.
questions.deeper: A strong candidate proposes a staged rollout after the offline suite: shadow mode where the agent suggests actions a human approves, then automatic handling of low-risk ticket types first. The approval and override rates from shadow mode are some of the best evidence for wider rollout.

questions.prompt: A chat platform trains a model to flag abusive messages. About 0.1% of messages are abusive. On a large test set the model has ROC-AUC 0.97 but PR-AUC (average precision) of only 0.18. A product manager asks how both numbers can be right. Which statement correctly explains the gap?
options: The false positive rate divides by the huge pool of clean messages, so even a tiny rate can swamp the few true hits.
PR-AUC is measured only at the default 0.5 threshold, so it misses the better thresholds that ROC-AUC averages over.
ROC-AUC also credits the model for ordering clean messages correctly among themselves, which inflates it when they dominate.
PR-AUC has a random baseline of 0.5, the same as ROC-AUC, so a score of 0.18 means the model ranks worse than chance.
questions.explanation:
ROC curves plot recall against the false positive rate, FP / (FP + TN). With 999 clean messages for every abusive one, TN is enormous, so even a large number of false alarms is a small rate. Precision has no TN term, so it shows those false alarms directly.

A worked case: 1,000,000 messages, 1,000 abusive. A threshold with recall 0.80 and a false positive rate of 1% catches 800 abusive messages but also flags 9,990 clean ones. That point looks excellent on a ROC curve, yet precision is 800 / 10,790, about 0.07.

PR-AUC is threshold-free like ROC-AUC, so the option about a 0.5 threshold is wrong. ROC-AUC is the chance that a random positive outranks a random negative. Pairs of two negatives never count, so it gives no credit for ordering clean messages. The random baseline for PR-AUC is the positive rate, 0.001 here, not 0.5. So 0.18 is far better than chance, just weak in absolute terms.
questions.deeper: In an interview, say which number matches the cost. If moderators review every flag, precision at the review budget is what matters, and PR-AUC tracks it better. A good follow-up is to report precision at a fixed recall, or recall at the number of flags the team can review each day.

questions.prompt: A support chatbot sends a 3,000-token system prompt that is identical on every request, followed by the user's message and some retrieved help articles. Replies average 300 tokens. Most traffic is simple questions such as order status and opening hours, yet every request goes to the largest model. Users say the bot feels slow, and the bill is too high. Which changes would cut cost, the delay users feel, or both, without a large drop in answer quality? Select all that apply.
options: Turn on prompt caching for the fixed system prompt, so that shared prefix is not processed again on every request.
Route simple, high-volume intents to a smaller and faster model, and send only the harder ones to the large model.
Stream the reply token by token, so users see the answer begin while the rest of it is still being generated.
Move the user's message ahead of the system prompt, so the model reads the question before the long instructions.
Ask the model to write out step-by-step reasoning before every reply, including simple lookups such as order status.
Lower the temperature to 0, because sampling from fewer candidate tokens makes each decoding step much faster.
questions.explanation:
Prompt caching reuses the work already done on a prompt prefix that repeats exactly. With 3,000 identical tokens at the front of every request, caching shortens the time to the first token, and it usually lowers input cost because the reused tokens need little new compute. Routing works because most traffic is easy. A small model answers "what are your opening hours" just as well, faster and for a fraction of the price, and the large model is kept for the hard cases. Streaming does not change cost, but it changes what users feel: they start reading within moments instead of waiting for all 300 tokens.

Moving the user's message to the front breaks caching. A prompt cache can only reuse a leading run of tokens that is identical to an earlier request, because the stored state for each token depends on every token before it. Once the varying text comes first, requests share almost no prefix and almost nothing can be reused. Step-by-step reasoning on every reply adds output tokens, and output tokens are generated one at a time, so it raises both latency and cost for questions that need no reasoning. Temperature only changes how the next token is picked from probabilities that have already been computed. The model does the same work per token at any temperature.
questions.deeper: A strong candidate asks for the latency breakdown first: time to first token, generation time and retrieval time. They also add semantic caching for repeated questions and set a quality check on the router, such as sampling small-model answers for review, so savings do not hide a quality drop.

questions.prompt: A research agent works through a task of about 200 steps. Each web page it reads adds thousands of tokens to its context. By step 80, cost per step has tripled, and the agent has started ignoring a constraint the user gave at the start: "only use sources from 2024 onward". Some page details will be needed again much later, when the agent writes its final report. Which memory design fits best?
options: Pin the constraints and plan in context, swap old page text for short notes, and keep full pages in a searchable store.
Keep the full history and move to a model with a larger context window, so every page and instruction stays in view.
Every 10 steps, summarize the whole history, constraints included, into one paragraph, and then drop everything else from the context.
Store every step in a vector database and keep only the latest step in context, so everything else is retrieved by similarity when needed.
questions.explanation:
Different information has different lifetimes, and the tiered design treats each kind on its own terms. The user's constraints and the plan matter at every step, so they stay pinned where the model always sees them. Raw page text matters mostly at the moment it is read, so it is replaced by short notes that keep the context small and the cost per step flat. The full pages go to an external store, so details the final report needs can be fetched back exactly when they are needed.

Keeping everything in a larger window does not fix the problem. Cost per step keeps growing with the history, and models tend to follow an early instruction less reliably as the context fills with unrelated text, which is the likely reason the constraint was ignored. Summarizing everything into one paragraph is lossy. The constraint may be shortened or dropped, and the page details the report needs are gone for good. Keeping only the latest step and retrieving by similarity sounds tidy, but the constraints and the plan are not similar to most individual steps, so they may never be retrieved, and the agent loses track of where it is in the task.
questions.deeper: In interviews, describe memory in tiers: working context, a running summary or scratchpad, and long-term storage with search. A strong candidate also mentions testing the design by checking whether the agent still follows early constraints late in long runs, since that failure is easy to miss.
